description: Somos QUORI, un equipo de estudiantes de la Tecnicatura Superior en Desarrollo de Software de Santiago del Estero. Tenemos el honor de representar a nuestro instituto y a nuestra comunidad educativa. Nos caracterizan el compromiso, la dedicación y el trabajo en equipo. Nuestra mayor fortaleza es el interés constante por aprender, adquirir nuevos conocimientos y asumir cada desafío como una oportunidad para crecer.
summary: ARTEMIS-MED is a biomedical monitoring console for a simulated Artemis IV lunar mission, built around NASA Human Research Program hazards such as radiation, CO₂ buildup, and spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS). The project includes a Python Flask backend that handles the mission logic, and a browser interface where three roles (crew member, chief medical officer, and commander) interact with an AI assistant called J.A.R.V.I.S. The assistant runs health check-ins, generates clinical protocols with step-by-step verification, and produces medical decisions for the commander. Users can simulate scenarios such as a solar storm, a CO₂ leak, or a SANS emergency, and export Standard Measures telemetry as JSON. The backend exposes a REST API, while the frontend uses a small JavaScript client to communicate with it. Together, the two parts show how a physiological monitoring system for deep-space missions could be organized.
details:
ARTEMIS-MED — Astronaut Health Self-Assessment Console

Educational prototype
All data is simulated, and all thresholds are team-defined heuristics. This is not a medical device and does not replace the guidance of a flight surgeon.

English summary: ARTEMIS-MED is a browser-based health self-assessment tool designed for astronauts on long-duration missions, using a Mars transit scenario. Crew members record blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep, exercise, and mood. The tool provides color-coded triage recommendations (self-management / notify the Crew Medical Officer / contact the flight surgeon), seven-day trends, an interactive body map with plain-language explanations, and offline functionality with a store-and-forward communication link to Earth. All data is simulated, and all thresholds are heuristic.

1. The Problem

During long-duration missions, astronauts are the first line of responsibility when it comes to detecting changes in their own health. NASA's Human Research Program (HRP) identifies five major hazards of human spaceflight:

  • Space radiation.
  • Isolation and confinement.
  • Distance from Earth.
  • Altered gravity fields.
  • Hostile and closed environments.

ARTEMIS-MED helps crew members measure, interpret, and act, supporting decisions about when to escalate a health concern to a crewmate, the Crew Medical Officer (CMO), or flight surgeons on Earth.

2. How It Addresses the Challenge

Challenge Question

ARTEMIS-MED's Approach

What health measurements can be taken in space?

A self-assessment form covering blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep, exercise, and mood. Each field displays its normal reference range.

Why is a health examination necessary?

An educational body-region dashboard explaining what each area represents, how it can be assessed in orbit, and why it matters.

How do spaceflight hazards affect these indicators?

A "5 Hazards" section explaining how the space environment affects each body region.

When should a concern be escalated to the CMO or flight surgeon?

A three-level traffic-light system displaying the reasons for each alert and the recommended action.

What actions can prevent a critical condition?

Three-step CMO protocols, countermeasures (ARED, hydration, sleep), and early detection through trend analysis.

Interactive human body figure

An astronaut illustration with seven interactive regions: eyes, heart, chest, spine, muscles, mood, and glucose/temperature.

Dynamic charts, color coding, and gamification

Seven-day trend charts, green/amber/red status indicators with text descriptions, streaks, and daily missions.

3. Main Features

  • Self-assessment: Astronauts enter their health measurements (Section 05), and the system immediately reassesses their status.
  • Escalation traffic-light system: Green (self-management), amber (notify the CMO), and red (contact the flight surgeon).
  • Trend detection: Analyzes seven-day trends in heart rate, sleep, exercise, mood, and glucose. Two or more converging warning signals trigger an early alert, even before an individual measurement crosses a predefined threshold.
  • Three operating modes: Crew Member, CMO (clinical checklist and data export), and Captain (crew protection decisions).
  • Autonomy under communication latency: An Earth communication link toggle. When disconnected, data packets are stored in a queue using a store-and-forward mechanism and transmitted once connectivity is restored.
  • Simulation scenarios: Nominal Operations, Solar Storm, High CO₂, and SANS Crisis.
  • AURA Copilot: Provides contextual answers and cross-references the astronaut's reported symptoms with available health data.
  • JSON Export: Exports the health log in a custom format inspired by NASA HRP Standard Measures (not an official NASA schema).
  • Accessibility: Status indicators never rely on color alone, controls have visible focus indicators, and the interface respects prefers-reduced-motion.

4. How to Run It

No installation or server is required. Simply open index.html in a modern browser (Chrome, Edge, or Firefox). Fonts are loaded from Google Fonts; system fonts are used when an internet connection is unavailable.

index.html Interface and screen logic
engine.js Rules engine: baseline, trends, escalation, protocols, health log
extras.js Forms, traffic-light system, educational dashboard, DTN link, gamification
styles.css Base styles
extras.css Styles for additional modules

5. Architecture

  • Edge/Offline: Everything runs directly in the browser, without a server. A real spacecraft system cannot depend on Earth-based connectivity due to communication latency (between 3 and 22 minutes each way for Mars missions).
  • Rules Engine (engine.js): Pure functions operating on mission state. Each health indicator is evaluated against predefined thresholds and the astronaut's personal seven-day baseline.
  • Interface (index.html, extras.js): Renders the selected astronaut's status and responds to newly entered measurements.
  • No Machine Learning: The system uses an expert system based on explicit, auditable rules rather than machine learning. This approach was chosen because every alert can be explained through its underlying criteria.

6. Prototype Thresholds (Heuristic, Not Clinical)

These values are not derived from an official NASA standard. They provide reasonable reference points for demonstration purposes and must be validated by medical professionals before any real-world application.

> 120 or < 40 bpm

> 125 or < 70 mg/dL

> 180 or < 60 mg/dL

Trend indicators:

  • Heart rate: increase of ≥ 1.2 bpm/day.
  • Sleep: decrease of ≥ 0.2 hours/day.
  • ARED exercise: decrease of ≥ 4 minutes/day.
  • Mood: decrease of ≥ 0.3 points/day.
  • Glucose: increase of ≥ 2 mg/dL/day.

The SANS risk level (Low, Moderate, High) is a prototype-specific scale. It is not a NASA clinical assessment scale and is based on self-reported symptoms and other available indicators.

7. Data and Privacy

  • All crew members, measurements, and simulation scenarios are fictional and generated by the team.
  • No information is transmitted to any server. In a real mission, crew medical data should remain locally stored and under the control of the CMO.
  • JSON exports are generated directly in the user's browser.

8. Known Limitations

  • No actual sensors are integrated. Measurements are entered manually or generated through simulation.
  • Thresholds are heuristic and have not undergone clinical validation.
  • Countermeasures (such as the antioxidant supplement included in the radiation protocol) are prototype proposals, not official NASA protocols.
  • The interface is currently available only in Spanish. An English version is still needed.
  • There are no automated tests in the repository. Verification was performed using manual scripts.

9. Extra References

Resources consulted from NASA's Human Research Program and the challenge materials (add the exact links from the "Resources" tab here):

  • Actigraphy and Sleep (ARCHeR).
  • Canadian Space Agency Neutron Sensor (CSA-CANS).
  • Radiation measurements during Mars transit using the RAD instrument aboard the Curiosity rover (reference for the approximate 1.8 mSv/day value used in the simulation).

10. Next Steps

  • English version and language selector.
  • Camera-based input (for example, ocular ultrasound or skin imaging).
  • Validation of thresholds with medical consultation.
  • Automated testing of the rules engine.
  • Integration with real sensors and export to a standardized health data format.

11. Team

  • Estanciero, Ivan Augusto.

  • Sosa, Ismael Augusto.

12. Disclaimer

ARTEMIS-MED is an educational project developed as part of a hackathon. It must not be used to make real medical decisions.
